                          INITIAL BRIEF OF G73 LANDOWNERS

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES (ALJ)                                                AND
COMMISSIONERS OF THE TEXAS PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION:


                                       I. INTRODUCTION

1. COME NOW, Intervenors Lazy B Land Company (Benjamin Tanner), Zymac Group (Randy
   Eldridge), RME Trust (Randy Eldridge), Randy & Tina Eldridge, Edd Melton, Jesse Priest,
   John Burrows, Paul Skinner and George Atkinson (collectively, "G73 Landowners"), owners
   and occupants of land within and adjacent to proposed route Link G73 in Bell County, and file
   this Joint Initial Brief after the close of evidence at the hearing on the merits. G73 Landowners
   respectfully request that the Administrative Law Judges and the Commission exclude Link
   G73 from any recommended or approved route in this proceeding.

2. G73 Landowners share a common and critical circumstance: every one of them owns or
   occupies property that is directly crossed by or lies within 500 feet of the centerline of proposed
   Link G73, and not one of them received the mailed pre-meeting notice required by 16 Tex.
   Admin. Code § 22.52(a)(4) before the 2025 public participation meetings at which route
   selections for this project were first publicly vetted. Their exclusion from that pre-application
   process was not accidental; it was the direct consequence of Applicants' failure to send required
   notice, a failure Applicants admitted on the record.

3. This brief proceeds in four parts. Part II addresses the mandatory procedural and notice
   consequences of Applicants' admitted notice failure and incorporates by reference the G73
   Landowners' Motion to Strike filed June 10, 2026. Part III describes the cumulative impacts of
   Link G73 on G73 Landowners' properties. Part IV addresses the cultural, historical, and
   archaeological resources at risk along the G73 corridor. Part V addresses why Link G73 cannot
   be justified on its merits under PURA's routing criteria. The conclusion requests appropriate
   relief.


II. MANDATORY PROCEDURAL AND NOTICE RELIEF - THE RULE'S REMEDY IS
                      NOT DISCRETIONARY

4. Title 16, Texas Administrative Code § 22.52(a)(4) requires applicants for electric transmission
   certificates to mail first-class notice of pre-application public meetings to the owner of land
   within 500 feet of the proposed route as reflected in the county tax rolls. The rule provides:

                                             Page 2 of 7
    "Failure to provide notice in accordance with this section will be cause for day-for-day
   extension of deadlines for intervention and for commission action on the application." This
   language is mandatory. The rule does not authorize the ALJs or the Commission to excuse a
   notice failure or decline to apply the remedy; it specifies the consequence directly.

5. During cross-examination on June 8, 2026, the first day of the hearing on the merits, Benjamin
   Tanner asked Applicants' representative directly: "A majority of link G-73 Landowners did not
   receive mail notice of the project until late March, 2026, correct?" The representative
   responded: "Yes, since that was an added link, after public participation meetings, that is
   correct." This admission is now part of the evidentiary record and is dispositive on the notice
   question. This admission establishes, without dispute, the factual predicate for mandatory relief
   under § 22.52(a)(4).

6. Applicants held three pre-application public meetings: June 16, 2025 in Salado, June 17, 2025
   in Lampasas, and June 18, 2025 in Menard. These meetings were the only pre-application
   opportunity for affected landowners to provide input before routing decisions were
   substantially framed. G73 Landowners received no notice of any of these meetings. Their first
   direct notification came in late March 2026, when the application had already been filed and
   preliminary route selections had long since been fixed. The window for meaningful pre-
   application participation that the notice requirement was designed to guarantee was
   permanently closed before these landowners ever knew it existed.

7. G73 Landowners respectfully urge the ALJs to apply the mandatory remedy specified in §
   22.52(a)(4). The statute and rule establish a public participation right that is meaningless if
   excused when violated. The purpose of the pre-application notice requirement is not merely to
   inform landowners of a pending proceeding, it is to give affected landowners a voice before
   route selections are substantially fixed, precisely so that landowners with knowledge of on-
   the-ground conditions, cultural resources, habitations, and environmental features can provide
   information that shapes the routing process at its earliest and most consequential stage. That
   opportunity cannot be restored retroactively after an application has been filed and a preferred
   route has been established.

8. For the reasons set forth in the G73 Landowners' Motion to Strike Link G73 from
   Consideration, or in the Alternative, for Day-for-Day Extension of Deadlines (filed June 10,
   2026, and incorporated herein by reference), the primary remedy is to strike Link G73 from
   further consideration in this proceeding. In the alternative, a day-for-day extension of not less
   than 283 days is mandatory, running from June 16, 2025 (the date of the first unnoticed public
   meeting) through late March 2026 (the date of effective actual notice to G73 Landowners).




                                            Page 3 of 7
  III. CUMULATIVE IMPACT OF LINK G73 ON G73 LANDOWNERS' PROPERTIES

9. Link G73 does not harm a single landowner in isolation. It affects a community of landowners
   whose properties, livelihoods, established uses, and long-term plans are each materially and
   adversely impacted by the proposed routing. Collectively, the G73 Landowners represent an
   interconnected set of affected properties along a corridor that Applicants never properly
   reviewed, never properly noticed, and never gave any opportunity for public input before fixing
   as a preferred route segment.

10. The property owned by Lazy B Land Company (Benjamin Tanner) is a 613.8-acre ranch that
    has been operated since 2015 as a no-cost, full-access nature and agritourism retreat for
    disabled veterans of the United States Armed Forces. The property is traversed across virtually
    its entire length by Link G73, which runs parallel to and within approximately 110 feet of the
    property's defining natural feature: a spring-fed creek, waterfall, and limestone sink. The
    property also contains an off-grid cabin built by hand between 2019 and 2024, located
    approximately 100 feet from the proposed right-of-way. Construction of a 765-kV
    transmission corridor adjacent to this feature would effectively destroy the veteran retreat use
    and cause material reduction in property value.

11. The other G73 Landowners, including Zymac Group and RME Trust (Randy Eldridge), Randy
    & Tina Eldridge, Edd Melton, John Burrows, and George Atkinson, similarly own or occupy
    land crossed by or within 500 feet of the Link G73 centerline. Each of these landowners was
    deprived of pre-application notice and pre-application participation rights by the same notice
    failure. Their properties, habitations, land uses, and established activities will each be
    materially affected by the proposed transmission corridor, and each has the same statutory
    entitlement to the relief requested herein.

12. The Commission's routing criteria under PURA § 37.056(c)(4) require consideration of
    impacts on landowners, habitable structures, environmental features, community values, and
    existing land use. Link G73 scores poorly across all of these criteria when properly evaluated
    against actual on-the-ground conditions, conditions that Applicants' desktop review methods
    were inadequate to reveal. Applicants' own witnesses acknowledged that their route analysis
    was conducted primarily through aerial mapping and highway-observable observations. The
    G73 corridor, which runs far from public roads through a variety of privately held properties
    with established and sensitive uses, was never subjected to a field-level review adequate to
    identify its impacts.

13. Applicants' habitation mapping also failed to capture the newly constructed residence of G73
    Landowner Jesse Priest at the north boundary of the Lazy B property, which is situated near,
    if not on, the proposed G73 right-of-way. This omission suggests that Applicants' habitation
    count for the G73 corridor may be understated, and that the comparison of Link G73 against
    alternative routes on this criterion may be inaccurate.



                                            Page 4 of 7
    IV. CULTURAL, HISTORICAL, AND ARCHAEOLOGICAL CONCERNS ALONG
                               LINK G73

14. The Lazy B Land Company property, George Atkinson’s property, Randy Eldridge’s property,
    and likely most other properties along the Link G73 corridor contain extensive surface
    evidence of prehistoric Native American occupation, including burned-rock midden features,
    chert debitage, projectile points, inscribed rocks, and other Archaic-period cultural materials
    concentrated along the spring-fed creek that runs parallel to the proposed right-of-way. The
    density of these materials, the geological setting, and the proximity to the Gault Archaeological
    Site (approximately six miles away), one of the most significant prehistoric sites in North
    American archaeology, collectively indicate a high-sensitivity archaeological area.

15. The G73 Landowners filed a Joint Statement of Position on June 7, 2026, addressing cultural,
    historical, and archaeological resource impacts associated with Link G73. These concerns are
    incorporated herein by reference. Construction of a 765-kV transmission corridor through the
    G73 corridor, involving heavy equipment, deep anchor installations for transmission tower
    footings, and extensive ground clearing, poses an acute risk of irreversible damage to intact
    archaeological deposits and potentially to human burials associated with Archaic occupations
    in this type of setting.

16. No professional cultural resources survey of the Link G73 corridor has been conducted.
    Applicants' environmental review of this corridor was conducted primarily through desktop
    analysis, without field investigation of the specific conditions along the route. This level of
    review is insufficient for a corridor with the characteristics observed along Link G73. Before
    any route incorporating Link G73 can lawfully be approved, a qualified professional cultural
    resources survey must be conducted and consultation with the Texas Historical Commission
    must occur as required by applicable law.


               V. LINK G73'S MERITS DO NOT JUSTIFY ITS INCLUSION

17. Even if the mandatory procedural remedy of striking Link G73 were not available, the
    Commission should decline to select any route incorporating Link G73 based on its
    independent demerits under PURA's routing criteria.

18. Link G73 was a "new link" added after the initial public meetings. It was not among the route
    links initially considered at the pre-application stage and was not subjected to the pre-
    application input process that other route segments received. Its addition to the project without
    proper notice to affected landowners effectively allowed Applicants to include a route segment
    that was never subjected to meaningful pre-application scrutiny.

19. The on-the-ground conditions along Link G73, including a sensitive natural riparian corridor,
    an active veteran retreat use, a potentially significant archaeological area, habitations including
                                             Page 5 of 7
    a hand-built off-grid cabin and a neighboring newly constructed residence not reflected in the
   project mapping, and a community of landowners who were never given the opportunity to
   present these facts at the pre-application stage are precisely the type of factors that PURA's
   routing criteria exist to weigh. When those factors are properly considered, they weigh strongly
   against the selection of Link G73.

20. The inclusion of Link G73 in any preferred route would reward Applicants for their failure to
    provide required pre-application notice, allow a route segment to be approved that was never
    subjected to proper pre-application review, place a 765-kV transmission corridor through a
    potentially irreplaceable archaeological resource without a required professional survey,
    destroy an established veteran retreat serving disabled veterans of the United States Armed
    Forces, and impose permanent harm on multiple landowners who were structurally excluded
    from the pre-application process. None of these outcomes is consistent with the public interest
    or with the Commission's statutory mandate.


                      VI. CONCLUSION AND PRAYER FOR RELIEF

WHEREFORE, PREMISES CONSIDERED, G73 Landowners including Lazy B Land Company
(Benjamin Tanner), Zymac Group (Randy Eldridge), RME Trust (Randy Eldridge), Randy & Tina
Eldridge, Edd Melton, Jesse Priest, John Burrows, Paul Skinner, and George Atkinson respectfully
request that the Administrative Law Judges and the Commission:

   1. STRIKE Link G73 from further consideration as a route or route segment in this
      proceeding, on the basis that Applicants failed to provide mandatory pre-meeting mail
      notice to G73 Landowners in violation of 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 22.52(a)(4);

   2. In the alternative, DENY any route incorporating Link G73 on the merits, based on the
      cumulative land use, habitation, cultural resource, archaeological, environmental, and
      aesthetic impacts documented in evidence and described herein;

   3. In the alternative, grant a day-for-day extension of all relevant deadlines pursuant to 16
      Tex. Admin. Code § 22.52(a)(4), running from June 16, 2025 through the date of effective
      actual notice to G73 Landowners (late March 2026), totaling not less than 283 days,
      applicable to the intervention deadline, the deadline for Commission action, and all other
      affected deadlines; AND

   4. Require that no route incorporating Link G73 be approved without a professional cultural
      resources survey conducted by a qualified archaeologist and formal consultation with the
      Texas Historical Commission; AND

   5. Grant G73 Landowners all other relief to which they may be entitled under PURA,
      applicable Commission rules, and applicable law.

                                                                              Respectfully submitted,

                                                  Lazy B Land Company, LLC (Benjamin Tanner)
